section.title: Healing the Leper and the Centurion
section.sectionRationale: Having taught with authority, Jesus now acts with authority. Matthew gathers a first set of healings: a leper cleansed by a touch, a Gentile centurion's servant healed by a word, Peter's mother-in-law raised from fever, and crowds delivered at evening. The section shows the King's power and willingness, and roots His healing ministry in Isaiah's Servant who bears our diseases.
section.thesis: The King who taught with authority now heals with authority and compassion, cleansing the untouchable, honoring the faith of an outsider above all Israel, and bearing the infirmities of His people as Isaiah's Suffering Servant, so that His power and His willingness to save are displayed together.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the leper cleansed by Jesus' touch; the centurion's great faith and the warning of a great reversal; Peter's mother-in-law healed; and the evening healings that fulfill Isaiah 53.

verses.text: When Jesus came down from the mountain, large crowds followed Him.
Suddenly a leper came and knelt before Him, saying, “Lord, if You are willing, You can make me {{katharizo|clean}}.”
Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man. “I am willing,” He said. “Be clean!” And immediately his leprosy was cleansed.
Then Jesus instructed him, “See that you don’t tell anyone. But go, show yourself to the priest and offer the gift prescribed by Moses, as a testimony to them.”
When Jesus had entered Capernaum, a centurion came and pleaded with Him,
“Lord, my servant lies at home, paralyzed and in terrible agony.”
“I will go and heal him,” Jesus replied.
The centurion answered, “Lord, I am not worthy to have You come under my roof. But just say the word, and my servant will be healed.
For I myself am a man under {{exousia|authority}}, with soldiers under me. I tell one to go, and he goes, and another to come, and he comes. I tell my servant to do something, and he does it.”
When Jesus heard this, He marveled and said to those following Him, “Truly I tell you, I have not found anyone in Israel with such great {{pistis|faith}}.
I say to you that many will come from the east and the west to share the banquet with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.
But the sons of the kingdom will be thrown into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”
Then Jesus said to the centurion, “Go! As you have believed, so will it be done for you.” And his servant was healed at that very hour.
When Jesus arrived at Peter’s house, He saw Peter’s mother-in-law sick in bed with a fever.
So He touched her hand, and the fever left her, and she got up and began to serve Him.
When evening came, many who were demon-possessed were brought to Jesus, and He drove out the spirits with a word and healed all the sick.
This was to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah: “He took up our {{astheneia|infirmities}} and carried our diseases.”

katharizo.gloss: To cleanse, make clean, purify. Leprosy made a person ceremonially unclean and untouchable; Jesus does not merely heal but cleanses, and stunningly He touches the leper, so that His holiness overcomes the defilement rather than being defiled by it.

exousia.gloss: Authority, right, power. The centurion understands authority: as his word commands soldiers, so Jesus' word commands sickness. He sees that Jesus need only speak, recognizing a power over disease that answers to Him as troops answer to a commander.

pistis.gloss: Faith, trust, reliance. Jesus marvels at the centurion's faith, greater than any in Israel, a trust that simply takes Jesus at His word. Matthew highlights that such faith, found in a Gentile, foreshadows the nations streaming into the kingdom.

astheneia.gloss: Weakness, infirmity, sickness. Matthew applies Isaiah 53:4 to Jesus' healings: He took up our infirmities. His power over disease flows from His mission to bear our brokenness, a mission that reaches its climax when He bears our sin on the cross.

basic.context: Jesus comes down from the mountain and immediately begins to heal. A leper, an outcast forbidden to be touched, kneels and trusts Jesus' willingness; Jesus touches him and makes him clean. A Roman centurion, a Gentile, asks Jesus only to say the word, and Jesus marvels at faith greater than any in Israel. He heals Peter's mother-in-law, then delivers and heals crowds at evening, fulfilling Isaiah's word about the Servant who bears our diseases.
basic.hermeneutics: Read these miracles as demonstrations of the authority Jesus just claimed in the Sermon, now shown in deed. Notice the pattern: Jesus is both able and willing, and He reaches the untouchable and the outsider. The quotation of Isaiah 53:4 tells us how to understand His healings: they flow from His mission as the Suffering Servant who takes our brokenness upon Himself.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus does not just heal the leper but makes him clean, overcoming the defilement with His holiness. The centurion grasps authority: as his word moves soldiers, Jesus' word moves disease. Jesus marvels at his faith, a simple trust that takes Him at His word. And Matthew says Jesus took up our infirmities, our weakness and sickness, fulfilling Isaiah's Servant.
basic.typology: Jesus cleansing the leper fulfills what the law could only diagnose; where Leviticus quarantined the unclean, Jesus removes uncleanness. The centurion coming from outside points to the nations sharing the banquet with Abraham. And the healings are signs of the Servant of Isaiah 53, who bears the diseases and, ultimately, the sins of His people.
basic.christ: Jesus is the holy One whose touch cleanses rather than being contaminated, the King whose mere word heals at a distance, and the Servant who carries our infirmities. He is willing as well as able. And He is the Lord of the messianic banquet, who welcomes believing outsiders and warns presumptuous insiders.
basic.god: God's power and compassion meet in Jesus' healings. The God who gave the law that excluded the leper now draws near in His Son to cleanse him. He honors faith wherever He finds it, even in a Gentile soldier, and He is bringing a kingdom that gathers people from east and west while it will exclude the presumptuous.
basic.crossReferences: Leviticus 13 and 14 give the law of leprosy behind the cleansing. Isaiah 53:4 is quoted, the Servant who bears our infirmities. Isaiah 25 pictures the banquet of the nations on God's mountain. And Matthew 15 shows another Gentile whose faith Jesus commends.
basic.oneStory: The King who spoke with authority now acts with authority and mercy. He cleanses the untouchable, heals at a word, and welcomes the faith of an outsider, warning that the kingdom will overturn every presumption. And Matthew tells us the meaning of it all: these healings are the first fruits of the Servant who takes our infirmities upon Himself, a mission that runs straight to the cross.

context.literary:
Matthew 8 opens the first of the great miracle cycles that fill chapters 8 and 9, and the cycle is arranged with care. The ten miracles fall into three groups of three, each group followed by teaching about discipleship or response, and Matthew 8:1 to 17 is the first group, with the leper, the centurion's servant and Peter's mother-in-law as its three healings, and a summary of evening healings closing the set. The Sermon ended with the crowds amazed at Jesus' words, Matthew 7:28; now the same hearers see the same authority at work. The word and the deed belong together, and Matthew tells us as much when he says, at 4:23, that Jesus went about 'teaching' and 'healing' in the same breath.

The three healings are chosen to cover the whole range of the unclean and the unreachable. A man excluded from the community for ritual impurity is touched. A Gentile, outside the covenant, is healed from a distance. A woman, in the privacy of a home, is raised by a touch of the hand. Matthew leaves out the details that fill his sources, the names, the elders who plead the centurion's case in Luke 7:3 to 5, the long narrative of Mark, and gives each scene a spare shape of request and answer. Each of the three people also begins by being at a distance from the main action, and each is reached by Jesus: the leper comes up, the centurion's servant is far away, and the fever lies in a house.

The quotation of Isaiah in verse 17 is the interpretive key. It is introduced by Matthew's characteristic formula, 'to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet,' and it comes at the end of the set so that all that has gone before reads in its light. The centurion's scene is also the centre of the passage, where Jesus' longest speech falls, and where the future of the kingdom, with Gentiles at table and the sons of the kingdom outside, is laid out in verses 11 and 12.
context.historical:
Leprosy in the Bible is not simply what a modern doctor calls Hansen's disease. The Hebrew word covers a range of skin conditions that made a person ritually unclean, and Leviticus 13 sets out how the priest was to examine them, with the footnote in the BSB simply calling it a skin disease. Someone who was declared unclean had to wear torn clothes, let the hair hang loose, cover the mouth, cry out 'Unclean, unclean!' and live alone outside the camp, Leviticus 13:45 and 46. Contact with such a person made another unclean. To the crowd the leper's approach would have been shocking, and his kneeling before Jesus more shocking still.

The ritual of cleansing in Leviticus 14 involved two live birds, cedar wood, scarlet yarn and hyssop, then a period of waiting, then offerings on the eighth day, Leviticus 14:4 and 10. The priest's examination was a certification of healing, not a means of healing. In all the Old Testament, only a few cases of cleansing are recorded, Miriam in Numbers 12:10 to 15 and Naaman in 2 Kings 5:14, and both were the work of God. When Jesus answers 'Be clean!' He steps into that tradition.

A centurion commanded a body of soldiers, nominally a hundred. He was a Gentile, a representative of the occupying power or its client ruler, and he lived at Capernaum, Jesus' base in Galilee, Matthew 4:13. His remark that he is 'not worthy' to have Jesus under his roof reflects the custom that a pious Jew avoided entering a Gentile's house, a custom Peter recalls in Acts 10:28. His grasp of authority comes from his own world: an order given by an officer carried the weight of the empire behind it.

Peter's mother-in-law shows that Peter was married, as 1 Corinthians 9:5 confirms for the apostles, and that a family household in Capernaum was the centre of Jesus' base. A fever could be serious in a world without medicine, and in her case recovery is described as instant: she rose and served.
context.canonical:
The leper's cleansing is the first of the 'lepers are cleansed' signs that Jesus will name for John the Baptist's doubting disciples, Matthew 11:5, a list drawn largely from Isaiah 35:5 and 6 and 61:1, with the lepers added. The Old Testament knew of such healing only rarely, and always as the work of God, so that when a king of Israel received a letter asking him to cure a leper, he tore his clothes and asked if he were God, 2 Kings 5:7. The cleansing at Jesus' touch thus answers the promised day of salvation.

The centurion's story reaches back to the promise to Abraham, 'all the families of the earth will be blessed through you,' Genesis 12:3, and to the prophets' vision of nations coming from the ends of the earth, Isaiah 49:12 and Malachi 1:11. The banquet Jesus names, with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob at its head, belongs with the feast 'for all the peoples' on the mountain of the LORD in Isaiah 25:6 to 9, where death is swallowed up and tears are wiped away. Luke 13:28 and 29 gives a form of the same saying at a different point in His ministry. The theme returns in Matthew 15:28, where another Gentile's faith is called great, and in the final commission to make disciples of all nations, Matthew 28:19. In Revelation 7:9 the multitude from every nation stands before the throne.

Isaiah 53:4 stands behind verse 17. Matthew's wording does not follow the Greek Old Testament closely, and many take it as his own translation of the Hebrew. Peter picks up the same chapter in 1 Peter 2:24, quoting 'by His stripes you are healed' from Isaiah 53:5, and applies it to sins. The healings in Matthew 8 and the cross of Matthew 27 are two sides of one work.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew wanted his readers to see that the authority of the Sermon was real, and that it came with compassion. After seven chapters of Jesus' words the reader is meant to see the same Jesus touch, speak and heal, so that no one could suppose that the teaching was merely an ideal.

He also wanted them to see the shape of those whom Jesus reaches. The first two cases are the ones who would be expected to be excluded, an unclean man and a Gentile, and both are met with immediate willingness. For a Jewish-Christian audience Matthew's point is that the doors of the kingdom are not closed by uncleanness or by birth, and a church that was beginning to receive Gentiles was to hear in the centurion a sign that this had always been the plan.

The warning in verse 12 completes the thought. If outsiders can enter by faith, then insiders can lose their place by lack of it. Matthew wants his readers to take heart and take care together.

Finally, he gives them the lens for reading every healing in the Gospel. When he says that Jesus 'took up our infirmities and carried our diseases,' he is telling them that these acts of mercy belong to the mission of the Servant of the LORD. They are not detached wonders but the early marks of a work that will end at the cross.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This passage describes what Jesus did on certain days in Galilee. It does not promise that every sick person who asks will be healed at once, and it does not say that the lack of healing shows a lack of faith. The centurion's faith and the leper's request are held up as models of trust, not as formulas that force a result. The leper himself says, 'if You are willing,' and Jesus' answer is His own free 'I am willing.'

The commands are few and clear. Jesus tells the leper to say nothing and to show himself to the priest, and that is a particular instruction for that man, not a rule for all who are healed. What carries over is the pattern: come to Jesus honestly, with the actual need, in trust that He is both able and willing. That the early church kept praying for the sick, James 5:14 and 15, and that Paul himself was not healed of his thorn, 2 Corinthians 12:7 to 9, shows that the passage is a sign of the kingdom, not a guarantee of an outcome on demand.

debates.question: Does Matthew 8:17 mean that physical healing is provided in the atonement?

views.label: Healings are signs of the Servant's work, whose fullness awaits the resurrection
views.case: Matthew applies Isaiah 53:4 to Jesus' healing ministry in Galilee, long before the cross, so the 'bearing' is bound up with His entering into human weakness and the sign of the kingdom, Matthew 11:5. Believers still sicken and die, as Paul himself knew, 2 Corinthians 12:7 to 9, and the final undoing of death is still future, 1 Corinthians 15:26 and Revelation 21:4. The healings are down payments.

views.label: Bodily healing is secured by the Servant's atoning work and may be claimed now
views.case: Isaiah 53:4 and 5 join the bearing of our sicknesses to the wounds that heal us, and Matthew quotes the first half in direct connection with healing. If the Servant bore diseases as He bore sin, some conclude that healing is as much provided as forgiveness, and may be asked for with expectation.

debates.bearing: Both views agree that Christ deals with the whole ruin that sin brought into the world, body and soul. The first holds that the full benefit of that work is not yet delivered to the body, and warns against promising a healing that Scripture does not promise before the resurrection.

debates.question: What is the 'testimony to them' in verse 4, and why the silence?

views.label: A witness to the priests that the Messiah has come
views.case: A priest who certified a cleansed leper, as Leviticus 14 required, would be presented with the evidence of a healing that only God could do. 'To them' would then be a testimony to the priestly establishment and to Israel. The silence is intended to prevent a premature, crowd-driven view of the Messiah.

views.label: A testimony against them, or a proof of Jesus' obedience to the law
views.case: The phrase can be read as a witness that Jesus honours Moses, setting right any charge that He treats the law lightly, Matthew 5:17. Others take it as a witness against the leaders who will not believe despite the evidence.

debates.bearing: Either way, the law is upheld and Jesus' power is publicly verifiable. His instruction to say nothing keeps the focus on who He is rather than on His fame as a healer.

debates.question: Who are the 'sons of the kingdom' in verse 12?

views.label: Those in Israel who presume on birth and privilege
views.case: They are the natural heirs of the promises. Verse 11 speaks of Gentiles taking their places at Abraham's table, and verse 12 of the heirs being cast out, which fits a warning against the presumption that descent from Abraham is enough, a warning John the Baptist has already given, Matthew 3:9.

views.label: Anyone, Jew or Gentile, who takes the kingdom for granted
views.case: The 'outer darkness' with 'weeping and gnashing of teeth' returns in Matthew 13:42, 22:13 and 25:30 for servants and guests who belonged to the household and were not ready. On this reading the warning stands for every era's insiders.

debates.bearing: Both readings hold that membership in a covenant people is not a substitute for faith, and that the kingdom's table is open to all who come to Jesus in trust.

study.originalLanguages:
The leper does something that Matthew often uses of worship. The verb is proskyneo, 'knelt' in the BSB, and Matthew uses it for the magi, 2:2, the disciples after the storm, 14:33, and the women at the resurrection, 28:9. It may mean only deep respect, but the leper's 'Lord,' kyrie, joins it. His request is carefully balanced on the verb thelo, 'to will': 'if You are willing, You can make me clean.' He does not doubt the power; he leaves the willingness to Jesus. And Jesus echoes the very word back: 'I am willing,' thelo. Between those two uses the touch comes, haptomai, the verb for a deliberate laying on of the hand, which should have made Jesus unclean under Leviticus 5:3.

The instruction to go to the priest ends with marturion, 'testimony,' and the gift is doron, the offering Moses prescribed. Mark's version records the same phrase, Mark 1:44. The word marturion is also used of the witness given in the Gospel to the nations, Matthew 24:14, so the leper's visit is a small anticipation of the way Jesus' works will be a witness in the world.

The centurion's address to Jesus is kyrie, and he calls his servant a pais, a word that can mean a child, a boy or a servant, and the BSB footnote notes the alternative 'child,' Matthew 8:6. His 'I am not worthy' is a form of hikanos, literally 'fit' or 'sufficient,' and the phrase 'just say the word' is, in the Greek, eipe logo, 'speak with a word.' The sentence that follows is an argument built from his own experience, a man under authority who commands others, and Jesus 'marveled,' thaumazo. The Gospels show Jesus marveling in two places, here at faith and in Nazareth at unbelief, Mark 6:6.

In verse 11 the Gentiles 'share the banquet,' from anaklino, 'to recline.' It is the verb for taking a place at table, as a guest of honour would. And 'the outer darkness' is skotos to exoteron, a phrase that appears again in Matthew 22:13 and 25:30.

The mother-in-law has a fever, from pyresso, and 'began to serve,' diakoneo, in a tense that points to ongoing action: her response to being raised was a life of service.

Verse 17 gives Isaiah's words through Matthew's own Greek. 'Took up' and 'carried' are lambano and bastazo. The Hebrew behind them is nasa and sabal, and nasa is the very verb used for the servant who 'bore the sin of many,' Isaiah 53:12, and for the goat that 'will carry on itself all their iniquities,' Leviticus 16:22. The bearing of diseases and the bearing of sin are the same word in Hebrew, which is why Matthew can say that the healings belong to the Servant's mission.

typology.fulfillment: The law could only diagnose leprosy and shut the afflicted outside the camp, Leviticus 13:45 and 46. Jesus does what the law could not do, removing the disease itself, and He does it by touching the man instead of recoiling from him. The leper's uncleanness does not pass to Jesus; His cleanness passes to the leper. This is the pattern of Christ's saving work, the pure one taking the place of the impure, 2 Corinthians 5:21. The type falls short at one point only: the leper was healed of an illness, and the deeper uncleanness of the heart remains for the cross to deal with, Hebrews 9:13 and 14.

typology.type: The centurion and the gathering of the nations
typology.fulfillment: The man from outside the covenant who trusts Jesus' word is a first fruit of the promise that all nations will be blessed in Abraham's seed, Genesis 12:3. The banquet of verse 11 is the feast of Isaiah 25:6 to 9, in which the LORD prepares a table for all peoples, swallows up death and wipes away tears. The correspondence is complete in one respect: Gentiles come in by faith, not by circumcision. The escalation is that it is Jesus who presides, and the table is at last opened. The type falls short in that this is still a sign; the full gathering is future, Revelation 7:9 and 19:9.

typology.type: The Servant who carries our diseases
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah's Servant is the one who bears the infirmities and sorrows of the people, Isaiah 53:4, and whose wounds heal them, Isaiah 53:5. Matthew sees the Servant's work already in Jesus' compassion in Capernaum. He fulfils it by entering into our weakness, Hebrews 4:15, and, supremely, by bearing sin on the tree, 1 Peter 2:24. The type falls short only in what it leaves unsaid: Isaiah's Servant was to be raised and exalted, Isaiah 52:13, and the healings in Galilee are earnests of that exaltation.

typology.type: The word that heals from a distance
typology.fulfillment: Psalm 107:20 says of the LORD, 'He sent forth His word and healed them.' The centurion's trust that Jesus need only say the word is a recognition of the very pattern the psalm describes. In Jesus the Word that heals is present in a person, and John's Gospel calls Him the Word, John 1:1 and 14. The correspondence is exact, and the escalation is that the word is no longer simply sent but is spoken by the one who is Himself God with us.

study.christ:
The three healings put three questions about Jesus and answer each one. Is He able? The leper's 'You can' is met by a word that works instantly. Is He willing? 'I am willing' is as personal a statement as the Gospel records. Is He near? He touches the unclean man, enters a fevered woman's room and takes her by the hand, and by a word reaches a servant he has never seen. Matthew wants the reader to see that Jesus is the one in whom power and tenderness are never at odds.

He is the holy one who cannot be defiled. Under the law, touching a leper made a man unclean. Here the transfer goes the other way. This is the pattern of the incarnation: He enters our condition without being corrupted by it, and what He touches He cleanses. The cross is where the pattern reaches its end, for there He bears what He did not deserve so that those who belong to Him may be made clean.

He is the Lord whose word is enough. The centurion understood what the scribes of the Sermon had not, that Jesus' word does not need the support of rituals or presence. Where a soldier's word carries the authority of Rome, Jesus' word carries the authority of the one who made the world, and the healing happens 'at that very hour.' Psalm 107:20 describes the LORD's word that heals; the Gospel identifies the speaker.

He is the Servant who bears. Matthew 8:17 is a statement about the cost: the Servant carries what He heals. Isaiah 53 reveals what lies behind the healings, that He takes the burden of the sick upon Himself. That is why the evening healings are not a distraction from the cross but its first fruits. He heals with compassion, and He heals as one who will carry, Isaiah 53:5 and 1 Peter 2:24.

He is the host of the great banquet. By promising that many will come from east and west to recline with Abraham, He places Himself as the one who decides who sits at the table. The Gospel's last verses show the same authority in the commission to all nations, Matthew 28:18 to 20. A caution is in order: the healed leper and the fevered woman are not allegories of every sinner, and the passage does not ask us to read hidden meanings into the birds of Leviticus 14 or the touch of the hand. It asks us to see in each healing the person who does them.
study.god:
The leper's prayer, 'if You are willing,' touches the oldest question people ask about God: is He able, and does He care? The passage shows that God's power and God's compassion are one. The God who gave the law that put the leper outside the camp is the God who comes in His Son to touch him. The law was not wrong; it did its work of diagnosing and protecting. But its God was always the God who longed to cleanse, and here He does.

God is a God who honours faith wherever He finds it. The centurion has no covenant, no synagogue membership of his own, and no sign to demand. He reasons from what he knows of authority and trusts that Jesus is the one in whom all authority is found. Jesus' astonishment is not the surprise of someone who has learned something new; it is the delight of the one who made the human heart to trust and finds it doing so. The same pleasure sounds in Matthew 15:28 and in Hebrews 11:6, 'without faith it is impossible to please God.'

God is a God who gathers. The promise to Abraham was never meant for one family alone. The nations coming from east and west, Psalm 107:3 and Isaiah 49:12, is the plan the Old Testament announced. The same passage shows that God's kindness is not blind to presumption. 'The sons of the kingdom' who count on privilege and have no faith will find themselves outside, and the God who welcomes the outsider is also the God who holds the insider to account, Luke 13:28 and 29.

God is a God who bears. Verse 17 does not allow us to think of divine healing as a distant wave of the hand. In Jesus, God enters our weakness and carries it. This means the sufferer does not face sickness alone, and it means that mercy has a cost that God Himself has paid.

For worship, the passage teaches a reverent boldness. We come with the leper's honesty, 'if You are willing,' and with the centurion's confidence, 'just say the word,' and we leave the outcome with the Lord who says 'I am willing.'

crossReferences.note: The rule for the person declared unclean: torn clothes, a covered mouth, the cry 'Unclean, unclean!' and life alone outside the camp. It shows how great a step the leper takes in coming to Jesus in front of a crowd, and how great the mercy is when Jesus touches him.

The law for the day of cleansing, with its two live birds, cedar, scarlet yarn and hyssop. Jesus sends the healed man to the priest to take part in exactly this ritual, so that the law is kept and the priest becomes the first witness to the fact that this disease has been healed.

Naaman, a Gentile commander, is cleansed of leprosy at the word of the prophet Elisha. The pairing of a leper and a Gentile soldier in Matthew 8 recalls this story, and Jesus Himself refers to Naaman in Luke 4:27. In Jesus, the cleansing is no longer sent through seven dips in the Jordan but given by a touch and a word.

Luke tells the centurion's story with the added detail that the centurion sent Jewish elders and then friends rather than coming himself. The two accounts agree on the words about authority and on Jesus' astonishment, and they show how a man can act through others and be said to have come.
'He sent forth His word and healed them.' The line describes the pattern of the centurion's request: a healing that needs no presence, only a word. In Jesus the word that heals is spoken in person.

The feast for all peoples on the LORD's mountain, where death is swallowed up and tears wiped away. This is the banquet of which Jesus speaks in Matthew 8:11, and it explains why the Gentile centurion's faith is a sign of the world's future.

The promise that 'all the families of the earth will be blessed' through Abraham. The coming of the nations 'from the east and the west' to Abraham's table is the fulfilment of the promise in the line of Abraham, which Matthew's genealogy began with, Matthew 1:1.

The Servant takes our infirmities and carries our sorrows, and by His stripes we are healed. Matthew uses the first half to explain the healings, and Peter uses the second to explain the cross. The two apostles read the one chapter as the story of one work.

A Canaanite woman's faith is called 'great' and her daughter is healed from that very hour, a phrase that echoes 8:13. Together with the centurion she forms a pair: two Gentiles in Matthew whose trust is greater than that of many in Israel.

John the Baptist's doubting disciples are told to report what they have seen: lepers cleansed, the lame walking, the good news preached. The works of Matthew 8 and 9 are here presented as evidence that Jesus is the One who was to come, drawn from Isaiah's picture of the kingdom.

Peter reads Isaiah 53 and says Christ 'bore our sins in His body on the tree,' ending with 'By His stripes you are healed.' It shows the apostolic reading that the Servant's bearing of sickness and of sin belong together and finds its fullest meaning at the cross.

study.oneStory:
The Bible began with a good world and a human race made to live in the presence of God. Sin broke that nearness, and the first sign of the break was exile: the pair sent out of the garden, Genesis 3:24. Leprosy in the law was a living picture of that exile, a person put outside the camp, cut off from the holy place and from the people, Leviticus 13:46. When a leper kneels to Jesus and is touched and made clean, the first reversal has begun. What sin removed, the King restores.

The story of Israel was also meant for the nations. God called Abraham so that all the families of the earth might be blessed, Genesis 12:3. For long centuries that promise was kept in the background while Israel kept the law and waited. Here, in a Galilean town, the first outsider walks in by faith, and Jesus announces that the feast Isaiah saw, with all peoples at one table, is coming. The warning goes with the promise. Israel's own history had shown that being the heirs of the promise did not guarantee a place, and the prophets said so, but here it is stated in the Lord's own voice.

The hinge of the whole is Isaiah 53:4. Matthew sees that the one who heals is the one who will bear. The same Servant who touches the leper will be 'numbered with the transgressors,' Isaiah 53:12, and will carry the sin and the sickness of the world to the cross. The healings are small previews of what will be done there. Death itself, the last enemy, is not yet destroyed, 1 Corinthians 15:26, and the evening crowds will be sick again and die. But what is begun in Capernaum is completed in the resurrection.

The end of the story is the feast and the wiping away of tears. Isaiah's banquet becomes the wedding supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9, with a multitude from every nation, Revelation 7:9, and there will be 'no more death or mourning or crying or pain,' Revelation 21:4. The leper, the soldier, the fevered woman and the crowd who came at evening will be found at that table, and the one who touched them will be the host.

quiz.q: What is striking about how Jesus healed the leper?

options.text: He touched the untouchable man and made him clean, His holiness overcoming the defilement.
options.note: Verse 3 shows Jesus touching the leper and cleansing him, reversing the law's quarantine.

options.text: He healed the leper from a distance with only a word.
options.note: That describes the centurion's servant; the leper Jesus actually touched.

options.text: He sent the leper to the priest before any healing occurred.
options.note: The cleansing came first by Jesus' touch; then He sent him to the priest as a testimony.

options.text: He declared that the leper was never really unclean.
options.note: The man was genuinely unclean; Jesus cleansed him, He did not deny the condition.

quiz.q: Why did Jesus marvel at the centurion?

options.text: His faith, trusting Jesus to heal by a word, was greater than any Jesus had found in Israel.
options.note: Verse 10 records Jesus marveling at faith unmatched in Israel.

options.text: He was a powerful Roman officer who humbled himself.
options.note: His humility is real, but Jesus specifically marvels at his faith, not merely his rank or humility.

options.text: He had memorized the law of Moses despite being a Gentile.
options.note: Nothing is said of his law-keeping; Jesus commends his faith in Jesus' word.

options.text: He offered a large payment for the healing.
options.note: No payment is mentioned; it was his faith that Jesus praised.

quiz.q: What did Jesus foretell about the messianic banquet?

options.text: Many will come from east and west to feast with the patriarchs, while presumptuous heirs are cast out.
options.note: Verses 11-12 announce the great reversal of outsiders welcomed and insiders excluded.

options.text: Only the descendants of Abraham will share the banquet.
options.note: The opposite; Jesus says many from the nations will come, while some heirs are shut out.

options.text: The banquet is only a symbol with no real gathering.
options.note: Jesus speaks of a real gathering in the kingdom, not a mere symbol.

options.text: No Gentile could ever enter the kingdom of heaven.
options.note: Jesus explicitly welcomes believing outsiders to the feast.

quiz.q: How does Matthew interpret Jesus' healings?

options.text: As fulfilling Isaiah 53:4, the Servant who took up our infirmities and carried our diseases.
options.note: Verse 17 ties the healings to the Suffering Servant of Isaiah 53.

options.text: As proof that Jesus was a uniquely gifted physician.
options.note: They show His divine authority, but Matthew roots them in the Servant's saving mission, not medical skill.

options.text: As unrelated signs with no deeper meaning.
options.note: Matthew gives them profound meaning by citing Isaiah, not treating them as random.

options.text: As a guarantee that no believer will ever be sick.
options.note: The healings are signs of the Servant's work; they do not promise no believer will ever be ill.

quiz.q: What does the whole section reveal about Jesus?

options.text: He is both able and willing to save, reaching the unclean and the outsider as the Servant who bears our brokenness.
options.note: The healings display His power, His willingness, and His Servant mission together.

options.text: He is a powerful healer chiefly interested in large crowds.
options.note: He does heal crowds, but the passage centers on His willing mercy and Servant identity, not crowd size.

options.text: He heals only respectable, religious insiders.
options.note: The opposite; He cleanses a leper and heals a Gentile's servant, reaching outsiders.

options.text: He is reluctant to help and must be persuaded each time.
options.note: He readily says I am willing and I will go; His willingness is emphasized.

questions: The leper said, Lord, if You are willing, and Jesus answered, I am willing. Where do you doubt not God's power but His willingness to help you, and how does Jesus' answer speak to that?
The centurion simply trusted Jesus' word. In what situation is God calling you to take Him at His word rather than needing to see or control the outcome?
Jesus warned that heritage without faith leads to exclusion, while an outsider's faith was welcomed. Where might you be presuming on background or religion instead of trusting Christ?
Peter's mother-in-law, once healed, got up and served. How does the healing and grace you have received move you to serve Jesus and others?
Jesus took up our infirmities on His way to bearing our sins. How does knowing your Savior carries your brokenness change the way you bring your weaknesses to Him?

translationNotes.note: A leper was one afflicted with a skin disease under Leviticus 13, rendering a person ceremonially unclean and socially excluded.
Servant may also be rendered child, or servant-boy, as the BSB footnote notes; the centurion pleads for a member of his household.
The quotation is Isaiah 53:4, from the fourth Servant Song, which Matthew applies to Jesus' healing ministry as the bearing of our infirmities.
